chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Khalid ibn Bukayr al-Taweel, who said:

My father called me when death approached him, and he said: 'O my son! Take hold of the wealth of your younger brothers, conduct business with it, take half the profit for yourself, and give them the other half. And there is no guarantee (liability) upon you.'

So the mother who gave birth to my father (his concubine) brought me before Ibn Abi Layla after my father's death, and she said to him: 'This one is eating the wealth of my son.' I said, so I narrated to him what my father had ordered me with. Ibn Abi Layla said: 'If your father ordered you with falsehood, I would not approve of it.' Then Ibn Abi Layla established a witness upon me: 'If I move it, then I am responsible for it.'

So I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) later, and I narrated to him my story, then I said to him: 'What do you see?' He said: 'As for the words of Ibn Abi Layla, I cannot refute them. And as for what is between you and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, there is no guarantee upon you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a father entrusting his son with the wealth of minor siblings for trade?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia juristic distinction between *daman* (financial liability/guarantee) and *zikr* (accountability) in the management of orphans' wealth. While the judge Ibn Abi Layli validated the arrangement in a civil context, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the son bears no financial liability (*daman*) for losses, yet remains spiritually accountable (*zikr*) to God for his stewardship, highlighting the nuance between legal immunity and divine responsibility.
